newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition launches tax reform bill.
newsitem.headline: German coalition launches tax reform bill.

text.p: The German government on Friday launched the first stage of major tax reforms in parliament as efforts to revive talks aimed at finding a compromise with the opposition appeared to have hit a dead end.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said quick passage of his 1998 tax bill and planned legislation for 1999 would give "a decisive push for a positive turnaround in the German business climate".
But he hit out at opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who quit talks on finding a tax deal in a row over coal subsidies, accusing them of holding up urgently-needed tax reforms.
"The delaying tactics of the SPD are harming the common good, the unemployed and those in Germany who still have work," Waigel told parliament's final session before the Easter break.

The 1998 tax bill foresees cutting the main corporate and commercial income tax rates and unifying them at a common 40 percent rate. The cuts would be neutral for revenue as they would be offset by tightening up on corporate write-offs.

The bill would also cut two points off the solidarity income tax surcharge to aid eastern Germany to 5.5 percent, lopping 7.5 billion marks ($4.4 billion) off the tax burden. The lion's share of income and corporate tax cuts would, however, come in separate legislation for 1999.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping said the coalition tax reforms would rip a huge hole in state finances and do nothing to cut unemployment, which is at a post-war record of 4.7 million.

Scharping added that the SPD would only rejoin the tax talks if the coalition met three conditions -- to slash the cost of employing labour this summer, cut taxes for ordinary workers next year and put together solid counter-financing for the tax reforms.
The SPD wants over half of non-welfare items pulled out of occupational insurance schemes from July this year as part of its strategy to boost consumer demand and stoke recovery.
"If you fulfil them we would be ready to talk, because we will have to talk any way," Scharping said, adding the two sides would be forced to hammer out a compromise eventually.
Failure to revive the tax negotiations would leave the two sides to slug it out in parliament's mediation process and the SPD could block the bill with its upper house majority.

Although Waigel repeated an invitation for talks to restart after Easter, there was little sign that either side was ready to sit down face to face after Chancellor Helmut Kohl turned down an SPD invitation to meet its leader, Oskar Lafontaine.
The SPD has said the coalition's sums on the revenue impact of the tax reforms do not add up.

The party's budget spokesman, Karl Diller, on Thursday said that if the reforms were implemented fully by 1999, Germany's budget deficit would overshoot targets required under European economic and monetary union (EMU) by quite an extent.
Diller's figures, based on official projections, predict a surge in the deficit to 174 billion marks in 1999 -- equivalent to 4.4 percent of gross domestic product.

That would be up from an official deficit target of 105 billion marks this year -- which just undercuts the Maastricht treaty's three percent limit. Diller said, however, he expected the deficit to hit 3.2 percent of GDP this year.
Some newspaper commentators on Friday said the talks were as good as dead already.
"The tax talks between the coalition and SPD have failed after the sobering exchange of letters between Oskar Lafontaine and Helmut Kohl," the daily Die Welt wrote.
And, even though the two sides are not that far apart on key points, "there is barely any chance that the dialogue will resume its previous form," the newspaper added.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-2609750
($ = 1.690 German Marks)
